hint_perihelion_long: Where perihelion (closest approach to the star) sits along the orbit, measured from the northern spring equinox: 90° = northern summer solstice, 270° = northern winter solstice. With a non-zero eccentricity this skews seasons between hemispheres — Earth ≈ 283° (perihelion in early January, softening northern winters). Irrelevant on a circular orbit.
climate_locked_note: Tidally locked — no day-night cycle, so the latitude climate model doesn't apply. Climate is set by the day/night terminator instead: scorching dayside, frozen nightside, a possibly habitable twilight ring.
share_modal_title: World link — select & copy. Anyone opening it gets these inputs
hint_star_mass_input: Star mass relative to the Sun. Determines everything: luminosity, temperature, lifetime, habitable zone. The Sun = 1. Red dwarfs 0.08–0.5, orange dwarfs 0.5–0.8, solar-type 0.8–1.2, hot stars 1.5+. Stars below 0.08 M☉ are brown dwarfs; above ~150 M☉ they are unstable.
hint_star_b_mass: Mass of the companion star. In binary systems, the secondary is usually less massive than the primary. Affects the combined luminosity and orbital dynamics of the pair.
hint_separation: Average distance between the two stars in the binary pair. Wider separation (>50 AU) makes S-type planetary orbits more stable. Close binaries (<1 AU) favor P-type (circumbinary) orbits.
hint_bin_eccentricity: Eccentricity of the binary stars' mutual orbit. High eccentricity reduces the stable zone for planets. Typical range: 0.0–0.8. Most binaries have eccentricity 0.3–0.6.
hint_luminosity: Total energy output relative to the Sun. Derived from mass via the mass-luminosity relation (L ∝ M^3.5 for main sequence). The Sun = 1. Determines habitable zone distance and planet temperatures.
hint_temperature: Surface temperature relative to the Sun (5778 K). Determines spectral class: O (>30000 K), B, A, F, G (Sun), K, M (<3700 K). Hotter stars are blue-white; cooler stars are red.
hint_radius_solar: Stellar radius relative to the Sun (696,000 km). Computed from luminosity and temperature: R = √(L) / T². Main-sequence stars range from 0.1 R☉ (red dwarfs) to 10+ R☉ (blue giants).
hint_lifetime: Time the star spends on the main sequence, relative to the Sun (~10 billion years). Massive stars burn out in millions of years; red dwarfs last trillions. Life needs at least 0.5–1 billion years to emerge.
hint_peak_wavelength: Wavelength of maximum emission (Wien's law: λ_max = 2,897,800 / T). The Sun peaks at ~502 nm (green-yellow). Determines what light reaches the planet and which photosynthetic pigments evolve.
hint_hz: Range of orbital distances where liquid water could exist on a rocky planet's surface. Inner edge: runaway greenhouse. Outer edge: CO₂ condensation. Depends on stellar luminosity.
hint_frost_line: Distance beyond which volatile compounds (water, ammonia, methane) condense into ice grains. Critical for planet formation: gas giants typically form beyond this line. ~2.7 AU for the Sun.
hint_sys_inner: Closest stable orbit around the star. Planets closer than this would be tidally disrupted or engulfed. Roughly 0.1–0.2 AU for solar-mass stars.
hint_sys_outer: Farthest stable orbit where the star's gravity dominates over galactic tidal forces. Defines the outer edge of the planetary system. Hundreds to thousands of AU for Sun-like stars.
hint_optimal_star: Stars between 0.6–1.4 M☉ are considered best for habitability. Lighter stars are too dim and tidally lock planets; heavier stars burn out too quickly for complex life to evolve.
hint_predicted_pigment: Predicted dominant color of photosynthetic organisms based on the star's spectrum (Kiang et al. 2007). Plants evolve pigments to absorb the most abundant wavelengths, reflecting what they don't need.
hint_absorbed_range: Wavelength range that flora would absorb for photosynthesis. Depends on the star's peak emission. On Earth, chlorophyll absorbs red (600–700 nm) and blue (400–500 nm).
hint_reflected_color: The color that plants would appear to an observer — the wavelengths they reflect rather than absorb. Earth flora reflects green because the Sun peaks near green-yellow.
hint_bin_period: Time for the two stars to complete one mutual orbit. Computed from separation and total mass via Kepler's third law. Ranges from days (close binaries) to millennia (wide pairs).
hint_combined_lum: Total luminosity of both stars together. Used to compute the combined habitable zone. Simply L_A + L_B for well-separated binaries.
hint_combined_hz: Habitable zone computed from the total luminosity of both stars. For S-type orbits, the planet mainly orbits one star, so the single-star HZ may be more relevant.
hint_s_type_max: Maximum stable orbital radius for a planet around one star in a binary system (Holman & Wiegert 1999). Planets beyond this distance are destabilized by the companion star's gravity.
hint_p_type_min: Minimum stable orbital radius for a circumbinary planet (Holman & Wiegert 1999). The planet must orbit far enough from both stars for its orbit to be stable.
hint_mass: Planet mass relative to Earth (5.97 × 10²⁴ kg). Determines gravity, atmosphere retention, and internal structure. Earth = 1, Mars ≈ 0.107, Neptune ≈ 17.1, Jupiter ≈ 317.8. Above ~10 M⊕ a planet starts accumulating thick gas envelopes.
hint_semi_major: Average distance from the host star — the semi-major axis of the orbital ellipse. Earth–Sun = 1 AU ≈ 149.6 million km. Determines the amount of starlight received, orbital period, and temperature.
hint_eccentricity: How elongated the orbit is. 0 = perfect circle, 1 = parabolic escape. Earth ≈ 0.017, Mars ≈ 0.093, Pluto ≈ 0.25. High eccentricity causes extreme seasonal temperature swings between perihelion and aphelion.
hint_axial_tilt: Angle between the planet's rotation axis and its orbital plane. Determines seasonal contrast. Earth = 23.4° (moderate seasons), Uranus ≈ 98° (extreme seasons), Venus ≈ 177° (retrograde, minimal seasons). Values 0–80° are considered habitable.
hint_star_mass: Mass of the host star relative to the Sun. Determines stellar luminosity, habitable zone location, and orbital period. The Sun = 1. Used together with semi-major axis to compute orbital mechanics.
hint_albedo: Fraction of incoming starlight reflected back to space (Bond albedo). Ranges 0–1. Earth ≈ 0.306 (clouds, ice, oceans), Venus ≈ 0.77 (thick clouds), Moon ≈ 0.12 (dark rock), Mars ≈ 0.25. Higher albedo → cooler planet.
hint_co2: Volume fraction of CO₂ in the atmosphere. Earth ≈ 0.0004 (420 ppm), Venus ≈ 0.965 (96.5%), Mars ≈ 0.953. CO₂ is the main greenhouse gas after water vapor. Even small increases cause significant warming.
hint_atmo_mass: Total atmosphere mass relative to Earth's (5.15 × 10¹⁸ kg). Controls surface pressure directly. Earth = 1, Mars ≈ 0.006 (thin, ~6 mbar), Venus ≈ 93 (crushing 93 bar), Titan ≈ 1.5.
hint_gravity: Surface gravitational acceleration relative to Earth (9.81 m/s²). Computed as g = M / R². Determines walking comfort, atmosphere retention, erosion rates, and maximum organism size. Mars ≈ 0.38, Jupiter ≈ 2.53.
hint_density: Average density relative to Earth (5.51 g/cm³). Indicates composition: <1 = mostly gas/ice, 1 = rocky like Earth, >1 = iron-rich core. Mars ≈ 0.71, Jupiter ≈ 0.24, Mercury ≈ 0.98.
hint_escape_velocity: Minimum speed to leave the planet's gravity, relative to Earth (11.19 km/s). Determines which atmospheric gases the planet can retain. Mars ≈ 0.45 (lost most atmosphere), Jupiter ≈ 5.32.
hint_surface_area: Total surface area relative to Earth (5.1 × 10⁸ km²). Proportional to R². Affects total habitable land area, ocean coverage, and biodiversity potential.
hint_volume: Total volume relative to Earth (1.08 × 10¹² km³). Proportional to R³. Related to internal heat budget and geological activity.
hint_aphelion: Farthest point from the star in the orbit. Computed as a × (1 + e). The planet receives least starlight at aphelion. Earth's aphelion ≈ 1.017 AU (July).
hint_perihelion: Closest point to the star in the orbit. Computed as a × (1 − e). The planet receives most starlight at perihelion. Earth's perihelion ≈ 0.983 AU (January).
hint_orbital_period: Time to complete one orbit (one year). Computed via Kepler's third law: P² = a³ / M_star. Earth = 1 year = 365.25 days. Mars ≈ 1.88 years, Jupiter ≈ 11.86 years.
hint_orbital_velocity: Average orbital speed relative to Earth (29.78 km/s). Faster orbits = closer to star or more massive star. Mercury ≈ 1.59, Mars ≈ 0.81.
hint_tropic: Latitude where the star reaches zenith at solstice. Equal to the axial tilt angle. Defines the tropics — the zone receiving direct overhead sunlight during the year. Earth: 23.4° (Tropic of Cancer/Capricorn).
hint_polar_circle: Latitude above which 24-hour daylight (or darkness) occurs at solstice. Equal to 90° − axial tilt. Earth: 66.6° (Arctic/Antarctic Circle). Smaller tilt = polar circles closer to poles = milder seasons.
hint_eq_temp: Temperature the planet would have with no atmosphere, based only on starlight and albedo. Earth ≈ 255 K (−18°C). The difference from actual temperature reveals the greenhouse effect's strength.
hint_greenhouse: Additional warming above equilibrium temperature from atmospheric greenhouse gases (mainly CO₂ and H₂O). Earth ≈ +33 K, Venus ≈ +510 K (runaway greenhouse), Mars ≈ +5 K.
hint_surface_temp: Estimated average surface temperature = equilibrium temp + greenhouse warming. Earth ≈ 288 K (15°C). Liquid water exists between ~273–373 K (0–100°C) at 1 atm pressure.
hint_surface_pressure: Atmospheric pressure at the surface, in Earth atmospheres. Computed from gravity and atmosphere mass. Earth = 1 atm (1013 mbar). Below 0.006 atm, liquid water cannot exist. Above ~10 atm, extreme conditions.
hint_scale_height: Altitude at which atmospheric pressure drops by a factor of e (≈2.718). Earth ≈ 8,500 m. Lower gravity → taller atmosphere. Affects cloud height, aircraft ceiling, and atmospheric escape rate.
hint_gas_retention: Which gases the atmosphere can retain, based on the Jeans escape criterion. A planet retains a gas if escape velocity > 6× the gas's thermal velocity at the exosphere. Lighter gases (H₂, He) escape most easily.
hint_in_hz: Whether the planet's orbit falls within the habitable zone — the range of distances from the star where liquid water could exist on a rocky surface. Based on stellar luminosity.
hint_habitable_tilt: Axial tilt between 0° and 80° is considered habitable. Extreme tilt (>80°) causes catastrophic temperature swings: polar regions bake while equator freezes, then reverses. Uranus-like tilt is hostile to complex life.
hint_system_age: Age of the star system in billions of years. Used to decide whether the planet has had enough time to become tidally locked. Solar System ≈ 4.6 Gyr. Life on Earth took ~1 Gyr to appear and ~4 Gyr for complex forms.
hint_tidal_lock_time: Order-of-magnitude time for stellar tides to stop the planet's rotation and lock one face toward the star (Gladman et al. 1996; assumes a rocky planet with ~12 h initial spin). Earth ≈ 10¹¹–10¹² yr (never locks); planets in the HZ of red dwarfs lock within ~1 Myr. Real values scatter by ~100×.
hint_avoids_tidal_lock: Whether the planet keeps its day-night cycle: lock time > system age. Tidally locked planets have a permanent scorching dayside and frozen nightside — habitability is only possible near the terminator or with a thick heat-redistributing atmosphere. Common around red dwarfs.
hint_climate: Energy-balance model: insolation per latitude from axial tilt, atmospheric heat transport and seasonal thermal damping calibrated to Earth. Ignores oceans, terrain, precipitation and orbital eccentricity — treat it as a first approximation. Summer/winter are solstice values.
hint_planet_mass_moon: Mass of the parent planet relative to Earth. Determines the Hill sphere (gravitational reach for moons), orbital periods of moons, and tidal effects. Earth = 1, Jupiter ≈ 317.8.
hint_planet_radius_moon: Radius of the parent planet relative to Earth (6,371 km). Used to express moon distances in planet radii and compute angular sizes. Earth = 1, Jupiter ≈ 11.2.
hint_planet_density_moon: Average density of the parent planet relative to Earth (5.51 g/cm³). Used in the Roche limit calculation — denser planets tear apart moons at closer distances.
hint_planet_semi_major_moon: Distance from the planet to its host star. Determines the Hill sphere radius — the region where the planet's gravity dominates and moons can exist stably.
hint_star_mass_moon: Mass of the star the planet orbits. Together with orbital distance, determines how far the planet's gravitational influence extends (Hill sphere).
hint_moon_radius: Moon's radius relative to Earth (6,371 km). Our Moon ≈ 0.273 R⊕ (1,737 km), Ganymede ≈ 0.413, Titan ≈ 0.404. Determines surface area, gravity, and angular size in the sky.
hint_moon_density: Moon's average density relative to Earth (5.51 g/cm³). Our Moon ≈ 0.606, Io ≈ 0.644, Europa ≈ 0.547. Rocky moons have higher density; icy moons are lighter. Affects mass and Roche limit.
hint_moon_distance: Distance from the planet's center, in planet radii. Our Moon ≈ 60.3 R⊕. Must be above the Roche limit (moon is torn apart) and below the stable orbit limit (~1/3 Hill sphere).
hint_hill_sphere: Maximum gravitational reach of the planet — the region where its gravity dominates over the star. Moons must orbit well within this boundary. Earth's Hill sphere ≈ 0.01 AU ≈ 235 R⊕.
hint_stable_orbit: Practical limit for stable moon orbits — roughly 1/3 to 1/2 of the Hill sphere. Moons beyond this are gradually stripped away by stellar perturbations.
hint_moon_mass: Moon's mass computed from radius and density: M = ρ × R³. Expressed in Earth masses. Our Moon ≈ 0.0123 M⊕, Ganymede ≈ 0.025, Titan ≈ 0.0225.
hint_moon_gravity: Surface gravity of the moon relative to Earth. Our Moon ≈ 0.166 g. Determines whether the moon can hold an atmosphere and affects potential habitability.
hint_angular_size: Apparent size of the moon as seen from the planet's surface. Our Moon ≈ 31' (arcminutes). Determines eclipses (≈ Sun's apparent size → total eclipses) and tidal effects.
hint_moon_period: Time for the moon to complete one orbit around the planet. Our Moon ≈ 27.3 days. Computed via Kepler's third law from orbital distance and planet mass. Determines tidal rhythms.
hint_roche_limit: Minimum safe distance from the planet, in planet radii. Below this, tidal forces tear the moon apart (forming rings). Depends on density ratio between planet and moon. ~2.5 Rp for equal densities.
hint_orbit_valid: Checks that the moon's orbit is physically possible: it must be above the Roche limit (not torn apart) and below the stable orbit limit (not stripped by the star). Both conditions must be met.
hint_multi_moon: Checks orbital spacing between moon pairs. Moons with orbital distance ratio <1.3 are too close and will gravitationally scatter each other. Also detects near-resonances (2:1, 3:2, etc.) which can amplify perturbations.
flora_reasoning_ob: Star peaks in extreme UV. Surface flora is unlikely without a substantial ozone layer. Underwater photosynthesis may use scattered visible light.
flora_reasoning_a: A-type star peaks in UV/blue. Flora would absorb the abundant blue and green photons, reflecting longer wavelengths. Plants would appear red or deep orange.
flora_reasoning_f: F-type star peaks in blue. Flora absorbs the dominant blue and green wavelengths, reflecting yellow-orange. Plants would appear orange or golden.
flora_reasoning_g: G-type star (like our Sun) peaks near green-yellow. Flora absorbs red and blue photons (most energy-efficient) while reflecting green. This is why Earth plants are green.
flora_reasoning_k: K-type star peaks in orange-red. Flora absorbs the dominant orange/red photons and most visible light, reflecting the least useful blue wavelengths. Plants would appear blue-purple.
flora_reasoning_m: M-dwarf star is dim and peaks in infrared. Flora must absorb every available photon across all visible wavelengths to gather enough energy. Plants would appear black or very dark purple.
ref_intro: What every input and output of the calculator actually means: in-depth articles on each property of the star, the planet and the moons — with Solar System examples and consequences for invented worlds. Click a heading to expand the article.
ref_star_mass_body:
Mass is the star's master dial: the calculator derives everything else from it — luminosity, temperature, color, radius and lifespan. It is measured in solar masses (M☉): red dwarfs are 0.08–0.5, the Sun is exactly 1, hot blue-white stars start around 1.5.
The worldbuilding rule: the heavier the star, the brighter it shines and the faster it burns out. A 2 M☉ star gives 11 times more light but lives under 2 billion years — barely enough for evolution to get started. A 0.3 M☉ dwarf will smolder steadily for hundreds of billions.
ref_luminosity_body:
Luminosity is the star's total radiated power across all wavelengths, in solar units (L☉). For main-sequence stars it climbs steeply with mass: L ∝ M³·⁵. Double the mass and you get an order of magnitude more light.
Luminosity draws the whole geography of the system: the habitable zone, the frost line and every other comfort distance scale as √L. A planet around a dim star has to huddle close — with all the consequences, tidal locking included.
ref_spectral_body:
Surface temperature sets the star's color and its letter in the O–B–A–F–G–K–M classification: from blue stars hotter than 30,000 K down to red dwarfs below 3,800 K. The Sun is a class G yellow dwarf (5,772 K). The astronomers' classic mnemonic: Oh Be A Fine Girl, Kiss Me.
The class is a ready-made palette for your world: the color of the sky and sunsets, the tint of noon light, even the hue of foliage (see Plant color). Under a K star the day is warm and amber; under an F star the light is harsher and whiter than Earth's.
ref_star_radius_body:
Radius is not an input — it follows from the Stefan–Boltzmann law: L = 4πR²σT⁴. Knowing the total power and how hot each square meter of surface is, we get the surface area, and from it the radius in solar radii (R☉).
Radius decides how the sun looks from the planet and how deep eclipses are in binary systems. Seen from a close-in habitable planet, a red dwarf can loom larger in the sky than our Sun: the star is small, but the planet hugs it tightly.
ref_lifetime_body:
A star lives while its core still has hydrogen: lifetime is fuel supply divided by burn rate, i.e. t ∝ M/L = M⁻²·⁵ in units of the Sun's ~10 billion years. A 1.5 M☉ star gets about 3.6 billion years; M dwarfs will outlast the current age of the Universe many times over.
For an inhabited world this is a hard deadline: Earth needed ~4 billion years to go from first cells to minds. A world around a bright F star may simply run out of time — its sun leaves the main sequence first.
ref_peak_wl_body:
Wien's displacement law: the hotter the body, the shorter the wavelength at which it shines brightest. The Sun peaks near 500 nm, in the blue-green; red dwarfs peak in the infrared, hot stars in the ultraviolet.
The peak is the key to biology: photosynthesis tunes itself to the most abundant light (hence the flora pigment prediction on the star tab), and evolution calibrates local eyes to the same maximum. A world around an M dwarf is a world of infrared vision.
ref_hz_body:
The habitable zone (the Goldilocks zone) is the ring of distances where starlight allows liquid water on the surface: from 0.95·√L to 1.37·√L AU. For the Sun that is 0.95–1.37 AU: Earth is inside, Venus already past the inner edge.
The zone is a guideline, not a guarantee. Mars sits almost at the edge yet is too small and lost its atmosphere; a planet inside the zone with a very high albedo will still freeze. What decides is the final surface temperature on the planet tab.
ref_frost_body:
The frost line (snow line) is the distance, 4.85·√L AU, beyond which water ice in the protoplanetary disk stops evaporating. Out there planetary embryos had several times more solid material, which is why giants grow beyond it: for the Sun it sits at ≈ 4.9 AU, with Jupiter right behind it.
It makes a handy survey line when designing a system: rocky worlds inside, giants and icy worlds outside. A giant found closer in (a hot Jupiter) is the trace of a migration that would most likely have thrown the small planets out.
ref_bounds_body:
The inner boundary, ≈ 0.1·M AU: any closer and the young star scorched and swept the dust away, leaving nothing for a planet to form from. The outer, ≈ 40·M AU: beyond it the disk is too thin and slow — nothing large can grow there within the system's lifetime.
These are boundaries of formation, not of travel: once born, a planet can migrate. But a system left the way it grew keeps all its orbits between these marks.
ref_star_hab_body:
The calculator treats 0.6–1.4 M☉ as the optimal range. Lighter, and the habitable zone is pressed against the star: the planet gets tidally locked and red-dwarf flares strip its atmosphere. Heavier, and the star lives too briefly and floods its planets with ultraviolet.
This is a risk marker, not a ban. Worlds around M dwarfs are science fiction's favorite playground (eternal day on one side!) — their habitability just comes with caveats and luck.
ref_binary_body:
About half the stars in the Galaxy come in pairs. A planet can orbit one star of the pair (S-type) or both at once (P-type, circumbinary — like Tatooine). The second star limits stable orbits: S-type has a maximum radius (roughly a quarter to a third of the stellar separation, less at high eccentricity), P-type a minimum one (2–4 times the separation).
The calculator gives both critical orbits, the combined luminosity and the pair's period. Keep the planet well clear of the limit: right at the boundary the orbit turns chaotic.
ref_flora_body:
Earth's foliage is green for a reason: chlorophyll greedily absorbs the Sun's red and blue light and reflects the spare middle of the spectrum — green. Around another star the balance shifts: photosynthesis tunes to its emission peak, and the reflected color changes.
The model predicts the pigment from the spectral class: under K stars foliage drifts toward blue-purple, around M dwarfs black is best — swallow every scrap of the meager light. Under harsh A and B stars surface flora struggles at all: without an ozone layer, photosynthesis hides underwater.
ref_ptype_body:
Mass in Earth masses (M⊕) sorts planets into types: up to 2 M⊕ rocky, up to 10 a sub-Neptune, up to 300 a gas giant, beyond that a super-Jovian. The radius can be entered by hand or left to an empirical mass–radius relation for each type.
The type answers the first question about any world: is there a surface to stand on? Sub-Neptunes and giants have none — surface area, volume and climate bands are not computed for them, and life is conceivable only in the cloud decks.
ref_gravity_body:
Surface gravity g ∝ M/R², in Earth units. Density (also relative to Earth) hints at composition: around 1 means rock and iron, well below it ice or a puffy atmosphere, above it a world with an enormous iron core.
For the inhabitants, g is everything: the build and skeleton of creatures, the height of mountains (which falls roughly as 1/g), the behavior of water, and the price of reaching space. At 2g birds struggle to fly — and rockets doubly so.
ref_escape_body:
Escape velocity, √(2GM/R), is the threshold for leaving the planet for good; Earth's is 11.2 km/s. The same threshold works against the atmosphere: when a gas's thermal speed approaches a sixth of escape velocity, that gas leaks into space over geological time.
Light molecules are the fastest: Earth cannot hold hydrogen or helium, while Jupiter holds everything. The gas retention table shows which atmospheres are possible at all; a world that cannot keep N₂ and H₂O stays dry and airless, whatever the habitable zone promises.
ref_orbit_a_body:
The semi-major axis a is the mean distance to the star in astronomical units (1 AU = the Earth–Sun distance). Kepler's third law gives the year: T = √(a³/M) years — the period grows faster than the distance. Orbital speed does the opposite: Mercury races at 47 km/s, Neptune crawls at 5.4.
The year is the rhythm of the whole world: the length of seasons, migration cycles, the calendars of civilizations. In the habitable zone of a red dwarf a year lasts Earth weeks: seasons never get going, but tides and eclipses beat time constantly.
ref_ecc_body:
Eccentricity e measures how stretched the orbit is: 0 is a circle, values near 1 a cigar. The closest point to the star is perihelion, a·(1−e); the farthest is aphelion, a·(1+e). Earth has e = 0.017 (the distance varies by only ±1.7%); Mars has 0.093, and it already shows in its climate.
The light flux changes as the square of distance: at e = 0.3 the planet receives 3.4 times more energy at perihelion than at aphelion. Such a world lives not by hemispheric winters and summers but by a great summer of the whole planet at once — the climate table shows how the seasons skew.
ref_peri_body:
Perihelion longitude answers the question: in which season is the planet closest to its star? It is measured from the northern hemisphere's spring equinox: 90° puts perihelion at northern summer, 270° at northern winter. Earth's is currently ≈ 283°: we are closest to the Sun in early January.
Hence the hemispheric asymmetry: the hemisphere whose summer coincides with perihelion gets a hotter summer and a colder winter — the contrast sharpens. That is how southern Mars lives: its overheated summer launches global dust storms.
ref_tilt: Axial tilt: seasons, tropics, polar circles
ref_tilt_body:
The tilt of the axis to the orbital plane is the engine of seasons: summer comes to the hemisphere leaning toward the star. It also draws the geography: the tropics lie at a latitude equal to the tilt (where the sun can stand at zenith), the polar circles at 90° minus the tilt (beyond them come polar day and night).
Earth's 23.4° is a sweet spot. At 0° seasons vanish and weather freezes in place. Past ~54° things get exotic: over a year the poles receive more heat than the equator. Beyond 90° the planet spins lying down or backwards, like Uranus; by Dole's criterion, tilts up to 80° count as comfortable.
ref_temp_body:
The equilibrium temperature is what the planet would measure with no atmosphere: a balance between absorbed starlight and its own thermal emission. Albedo is the fraction of light reflected (0.3 for Earth, ~0.75 for cloudy Venus): the whiter the world, the colder it is, all else being equal.
Greenhouse gases return part of the outgoing heat to the surface — that is exactly the difference between the equilibrium and the true temperature. The greenhouse gives Earth +33 K (without it: −18 °C and global ice), and Venus hundreds of degrees. The CO₂ and atmosphere-mass dials control precisely this bonus.
ref_atmo_body:
Surface pressure is estimated from the atmosphere's mass and gravity: the same gas presses harder on a high-g planet. The scale height is how many kilometers of altitude it takes for pressure to drop by a factor of e ≈ 2.72: about 8.5 km on Earth, more on light Mars, while heavy worlds keep their atmosphere pinned in a thin layer.
Scale height sets the altitude of cloud decks and flight, how quickly mountains rise out of the atmosphere, and the color of the sky on the summits. On a world with a small scale height, the high ridges poke into near-space.
ref_tidal_body:
The star's tidal forces brake the planet's spin until a day equals a year — then the planet faces its star with one side forever, like the Moon faces Earth. The locking time is wildly sensitive to distance (∝ a⁶): a little closer means millions of years, a little farther means never.
The calculator compares the locking time with the system's age. A locked world is eternal day on one side, eternal night on the other, and a ring of twilight between; latitude climate bands do not apply to it, as the planet tab honestly warns.
ref_climate_body:
The model slices the planet into 15° latitude bands and computes for each the annual insolation (axial tilt + eccentricity + perihelion longitude), atmospheric heat transport and the seasonal swing. From its summer and winter temperatures each band gets a simplified Köppen class — from tropics to ice cap, plus a scorched class for worlds hotter than any life.
The disc next to the table is the planet's portrait: the colored stripes are the bands, and the tabs switch between hemispheres. Play with the tilt and the eccentricity — the band map responds instantly.
ref_age_body:
The age in billions of years (Gyr) is the judge in two questions: has the planet had time to become tidally locked, and has life had time to grow complex. The Solar System is 4.6 billion years old; Earth's oxygen atmosphere and multicellular life took billions of years of evolution.
A young system also means bombardment: for the first few hundred million years the orbits are not yet swept clean, sterilizing impacts are routine, and moons and rings are still taking shape.
ref_hill_body:
The Hill sphere is the region where the planet's pull beats the star's tidal influence: r = a·∛(m/3M). Inside it the planet can in principle keep moons, but orbits near the edge are short-lived, so the practical ceiling is half the Hill sphere.
Earth's Hill sphere is ≈ 235 planet radii, and the Moon sits at 60 — deep and safe. The closer the planet to its star and the lighter it is, the smaller the sphere: around Mercury, moons simply do not survive.
ref_roche_body:
The Roche limit is the distance below which the planet's tides tear a satellite apart faster than its own gravity can hold it together: ≈ 2.44·R·∛(planet ρ / moon ρ) for loosely bound bodies. A monolithic rock can edge a bit closer — but not for long.
A moon past the limit does not fall — it smears into a ring: all the great rings of the giants lie inside their Roche limits. Want your world to have rings? Move a moon in, or break one.
ref_moon_props_body:
The moon's mass is derived from its radius and density (both in Earth units): M = ρ·R³. Our Moon: radius 0.273 R⊕ and density 0.606 ρ⊕ give 0.0123 M⊕ and gravity 0.166 g — one sixth of Earth's.
Gravity decides whether the moon can keep an atmosphere and how colonists' jumps look. And the moon-to-planet mass ratio sets the strength of the return tides: our Moon is anomalously large — hence the powerful ocean tides and the stabilized tilt of Earth's axis.
ref_moon_sky: Angular size: the moon in the sky
ref_moon_sky_body:
Angular size is how big the satellite looks from the surface: diameter divided by distance, in arcminutes. Our Moon and Sun are both about 30′ (half a degree) — a rare coincidence that gives us total eclipses with a visible corona.
A 60′ satellite is twice the Moon's width and floods the night with light; a 5′ one is just a bright dot. Compare it with the angular size of the local sun: if the moon is larger, total eclipses are frequent; if smaller, only annular ones happen.
ref_moon_period_body:
The period follows Kepler's third law from the distance (in planet radii) and the planet's mass. The Moon at 60.3 R⊕ circles Earth in 27.3 days — that is where the month came from as a unit of time.
The moon's period is a culture's metronome: months, tides, night navigation and hunting by phases. A close moon with a period of a couple of days brings furious tides and a sky where the phase changes before your eyes.
ref_moon_multi_body:
Two moons are too crowded if their distances from the planet differ by less than a factor of 1.3 — the calculator marks such pairs as too close. A crowded pair has one ending: a collision, or one moon thrown out.
A separate badge marks resonance: the periods relate as small whole numbers (2:1, 3:2, 5:3…), so the gravitational nudges repeat in the same phase. Resonance can stabilize a system (Io–Europa–Ganymede at Jupiter) or pump an orbit up — and it heats interiors with tides along the way: Io's volcanoes are paid for by exactly this.
